king who teaches the five fires
sage of the meditation on Brahman

stories.title: Naciketas and Death
stories.summary: A boy given away to Death waits three nights at his door, is offered every pleasure in exchange for his question, and refuses them all.

stories.title: Indra and Virocana
stories.summary: Two students hear Prajāpati's first answer. Virocana leaves satisfied and teaches it to his people; Indra sees the flaw, returns three times, and is taught the truth after a hundred and one years.

stories.title: Satyakāma tells the truth
stories.summary: Asked his lineage, a boy repeats his mother's honest answer that she does not know it. The teacher accepts him because he did not swerve from the truth.

stories.title: Uddālaka teaches Śvetaketu: “that thou art”
stories.summary: Śvetaketu returns from twelve years of study, proud and unable to say what makes the unheard heard. His father teaches him with clay, honey, rivers, a tree, a banyan seed and salt dissolved in water, and nine times says: that thou art.

stories.title: Nārada knows the texts
stories.summary: Nārada lists every science he has mastered and admits he is still in sorrow: he knows the words, not the Self. Sanatkumāra leads him to the boundless.

stories.title: Maitreyī's question
stories.summary: Offered half of a household's wealth, Maitreyī asks the only question that matters: 'What should I do with that which will not make me immortal?'

stories.title: Bhṛgu learns by inquiry
stories.summary: Bhṛgu asks his father for Brahman. Varuṇa gives him clues and sends him to find out. Five times Bhṛgu returns with a deeper answer, until he reaches bliss.

stories.title: The gods and the Yakṣa
stories.summary: The gods take a victory for their own. A mysterious being sets a blade of grass before Agni and Vāyu, who cannot burn or move it. Umā tells Indra who it was.

stories.title: Sukeśa will not lie
stories.summary: Sukeśa tells his teacher Pippalāda how a prince once asked him about the person of sixteen parts, and how he answered plainly that he did not know, because one who speaks untruth withers to the root.

stories.title: Gārgī questions Yājñavalkya
stories.summary: At Janaka's great debate, Gārgī presses Yājñavalkya on what the worlds are woven upon until he warns her not to ask too far; she returns with two questions like arrows and is answered with the Imperishable.

stories.title: Janaka and the light of the person
stories.summary: King Janaka asks Yājñavalkya what light a person has: the sun, the moon, fire, speech; and when all are gone, the Self is the light.

stories.title: Six seekers before Pippalāda
stories.summary: Six students come to the sage Pippalāda with fuel in hand. He makes them live a year in austerity, then answers six questions: on creation, breath, its rising and setting, sleep, OM and the Person of sixteen parts.

stories.title: Śaunaka asks Aṅgiras
stories.summary: The great householder Śaunaka asks: what is that by knowing which all this is known? Aṅgiras answers with the two knowledges, the lower and the higher.

stories.title: Jānaśruti and Raikva the cart-man
stories.summary: A generous king overhears two swans praising a sage who sits under a cart scratching his itch. He offers cattle and gold; Raikva sends him away until he comes with real humility.

stories.title: Upakosala and the fires
stories.summary: A student tends his teacher's fires for twelve years and falls ill with longing; the fires themselves teach him that Brahman is breath, joy and space.

stories.title: Aśvapati and the universal self
stories.summary: Five learned householders and Uddālaka go to King Aśvapati, each worshipping a part of the self; he teaches them the self that is all of it.

stories.title: Pravāhaṇa and the five fires
stories.summary: Śvetaketu, proud of his learning, cannot answer King Pravāhaṇa's five questions about where beings go after death. His father comes humbly to learn the teaching of the five fires.

stories.title: Ajātaśatru and the proud Bālāki
stories.summary: Bālāki offers to teach the king Brahman and names twelve forms of it; each is refuted, and the king leads him to a sleeping man to show where the self goes in sleep.

stories.title: Citra questions Śvetaketu
stories.summary: King Citra asks the young priest where the worlds after death end; neither son nor father knows, and both come to learn from the king.

stories.title: Indra teaches Pratardana
stories.summary: The king Pratardana wins his way to Indra's world and asks for the boon most beneficial to humans; Indra teaches him that he is prāṇa, the conscious self.

stories.title: King Bṛhadratha in the forest
stories.summary: Weary of a body made of bones, skin and decay, King Bṛhadratha gives up his kingdom and stands a thousand years in austerity until the sage Śākāyanya teaches him the Self.

stories.title: The Self creates the worlds
stories.summary: In the beginning the Self alone was; it thought, let me create the worlds, then their guardians, then food; and finally it entered the person through the crown of the head.

stories.title: Uṣasti eats the elephant-keeper's beans
stories.summary: In a famine a starving priest eats an elephant-keeper's leftover beans but refuses his water: one bends a rule to live, not for comfort. He then questions the court priests on the gods they chant to.

stories.title: The thunder says Da, Da, Da
stories.summary: Gods, humans and demons ask Prajāpati for teaching; to each he says only 'Da'. The gods hear restrain, the humans give, the demons be compassionate, and the thunder repeats it still.

stories.title: Śāṇḍilya's meditation
stories.summary: All this is Brahman. The self within the heart is smaller than a grain of rice and greater than the earth: Śāṇḍilya's teaching on how to meditate on it.

stories.title: Yājñavalkya at Janaka's court
stories.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the most learned of the Brahmins. Yājñavalkya has them driven away before anyone answers; one by one the court's scholars question him, from Aśvala to Gārgī and Śākalya, and none prevails.

stories.title: The gods, the demons and the breath
stories.summary: The gods chant the Udgītha to overcome the demons; each sense chants and is pierced by evil, until the breath in the mouth chants and the demons shatter against it like clods against a rock.

stories.title: The dogs' Udgītha
stories.summary: A satire on ritual for gain: hungry dogs ask a white dog to chant the Udgītha for food, and parade like priests before the hymn: ‘Om, let us eat! Om, let us drink!’

stories.title: Three sages on the Udgītha
stories.summary: Three learned men ask one another what the chant rests on; each answer is taken one step further, from heaven to space, until King Pravāhaṇa names space as the final support.
